****MEGA**** (Why do people write that? Duh, it’s a super rare bird. Tell me something I don’t know).     Kudos to Marty for noticing/finding this bird. 37°31′28″ N  122°30′14″ W Green mantle, pale ventral surfaces. Typical Phylloscopus warbler in size and shape. The bird was even more active than a kinglet. Very difficult if not impossible to photograph so we decide as a just enjoy watching it and let others torture themselves. Legs and feet the same dirty yellow color along their entire length. Obvious supercilium. Wing bars. This bird was not a Pallas’s Leaf Warbler (which has an even more elaborate head pattern). Please read Marty’s description for a why this was not a Hume’s Warbler. Park on Ranch Road and walk up the dirt road (5 minute walk) to the above GPS coordinates. We could not hear the bird the entire time we were there because a large number of the birders present kept talking nonstop about topics not even related to this bird. The failure of this many murders to understand that they’re keeping the rest of us from hearing or possibly even recording the bird was infuriating. One birder had such a loud voice that even when he walked 100 feet or more away from the crowd for his important phone call, we could still hear and understand every word he was saying. Also, it is our understanding that they crowded a lot closer to the trees, where the bird has been, which probably caused it to stay deeper in the trees and bushes and more difficult to see. This was a nice North American bird for Tom.

Outstanding find by Marty Freeland! A small, grayish-green, kinglet-like warbler with a small bill with some yellow, a long, pale, high-contrast supercilium, and two wing bars. It gave occasional high-pitched “suweet” calls as it foraged frantically deep in the willows, making looping flycatching sallies. Possibly the worst photos of the m.ob.

LFM notes: astoundingly small and fast-moving, even more so than RCKI. While superficially kinglet-like, this bird stood out as more "long" than "round", with paler underparts, and an obvious pale eyebrow, mostly white and maybe slightly yellow toward forehead. Upperparts had some distinct greenish yellow, and also showed a dark "kinglet bar" behind the second white wingbar. In certain binocular views at certain angles, the auricular appeared somewhat stippled and the pale throat looked lightly streaked with dark gray. Lower mandible of bill about 2/3s pale orange at the base. Legs pale. Foraging behavior frantic, rarely sitting still for more than a couple seconds. Often would drop and do a looping flycatching maneuver, circling quickly back up to the spot it left. Calls heard were a joyous, whistled "su-weet!" slightly reminiscent of Western Flycatcher, sometimes while foraging but definitely the few times it flew between willow patches.

The presence of two wingbars eliminates many Phylloscopus. The possible similar species would be Two-barred (would show longer tail, larger more obvious orangey bill, and would lack "kinglet bar"), Hume's Leaf-Warbler (would be duller, with darker bill and legs), and Pallas's Leaf-Warbler (would have much bolder head pattern with median crown stripe, and smaller bill). The call heard numerous times also helps eliminate many other possible species.

Small-to-medium Phylloscopus warbler with broad, creamy eyeline and wing bars (two) to match. Small, orange-based bill; gray crown without obvious median stripe; crisp, sooty line through eye. Upper back olive-brown; primaries and lower back with a hint of yellow. Flanks and belly creamy-gray, perhaps with a very light yellow cast (though it was tough to see with the bird backlit, against the sky for much of my vigil). Tail gray and without any white. The wing bars rule out Dusky, Arctic, and Kamchatka Leaf Warblers; Pallas's Leaf Warbler is smaller with yellow lines on head/face an an obvious pale rump.  A quick, upsweeping two syllable 'suwee' call, given at long intervals, eliminated Hume's and Two-barred. Bay Area bike bird #376. San Mateo County bike bird #310. When I arrived at Marty's coordinates about a dozen birders were watching the bird flit about in the willow riparian canopy. When I finally got a decent look I was struck by the bold patterns on this bird, especially compared to other Phylloscopus warblers I have seen in California (Dusky and Willow). While scoping to the N just beyond the surfers in the rear surf @ 9:25, a dark shearwater suddenly entered my field of view heading S low over the water then arcing up and down over the swells repeatedly. It was in my scope view for just under a minute as it continued heading S until out of view. As it was not very far out and there was no sun glare in the overcast conditions, I had excellent views as it went up and down over the swells. Rather dark upperparts and underparts, including an almost uniform underwing without contrasty white flash. In scope views its head looked short and rounded, almost fulmar-like (it was not a fulmar with its shearwater bill and wing structure). What really stood out to me was its rather buoyant, light flight and arcing over the waves on a morning with not much wind -- different to my eyes than the flight-style of Sooties. Also interesting that it was a solo individual, much closer to shore than I usually observe shearwaters from this seawatch. The last Sooties from the seawatch were back on 9/28.

An amazing experience with a moderately dull bird, initially at (37.7702658, -122.4763537). It then worked east along the lakeshore halfway to the concrete bridge before flying north across the street to the thick stuff at the top of the Log Cabin Trail hill, where I lost it. It was then not seen until Dario refound it at sunset back in the lakeside willows, which I would imagine are the best place to look. It was giving a loud, sweet, slightly breathy chip, kind of like a weaker California Towhee, intermediate in quality between Hooded and Orange-crowned warblers. 

A very large warbler, mainly rich saturated yellow in color with a white crissum and slate-blue wings and tail, duller yellow on the face and above grading into greenish-yellow on the back, large eye and bill on otherwise blank face (maybe slightly dusky lores?), a rather blank facial expression, striking undertail pattern slightly reminiscent of Magnolia, mainly white from the underside with black tips/edges, forming an interesting pattern when spread. Very little white visible from above, suggesting HY (in combination with its also being rather dull), but views and photos did not permit seeing whether white was limited to the three outermost rectrices or not. Cooperative when in lakeside willows and rather slow-moving. I first saw its face staring me down, and seeing the bright yellow face of a medium, large-billed, blank-faced passerine, it looked almost like an Orchard Oriole. And then a microsecond later it looked obviously like a Prothonotary Warbler and tripled my heart rate and all that! This was my first self-found Protho and my most wanted self-find (proportional to actual rarity) in the state and an absolutely electric experience. Photos.
